Tech Report: Jude Bellingham scores 'the best goal of my life' as his stunning long-range volley helps Real Madrid come from behind to thump PSV Eindhoven 5-1 in the Champions League

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Published: 18:45 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:20 EST, 25 November 2026.
  • Jude Bellingham underlined his class once more with a stunning goal as Real Madrid came from behind to thump PSV Eindhoven 5-1.
  • With Real trailing 1-0 at half-time, the England superstar - who started as a substitute to rest - was one of three changes made by Jose Mourinho and his impact was felt 15 minutes later in an emphatic style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By LUKE AUGUSTUS, ASSISTANT SPORTS EDITOR.

Published: 18:45 EST, 24 November 2026 | Updated: 03:20 EST, 25 November 2026.

Jude Bellingham underlined his class once more with a stunning goal as Real Madrid came from behind to thump PSV Eindhoven 5-1.

With Real trailing 1-0 at half-time, the England superstar - who started as a substitute to rest - was one of three changes made by Jose Mourinho and his impact was felt 15 minutes later in an emphatic style.

Sources indicate that collecting a loose ball from around 25 yards outside the box, Bellingham controlled it with his left foot, before flicking it up with his right foot and volleying it with the outside of that boot into the far corner of the PSV goal. The pace and precision of the strike was breathtaking as it flew past Matej Kovar and hit the inside of the post before going in.

It was a strike that was befitting of any match, and it proved to be the decisive one as that made it 2-1 to the hosts before they later ran riot.

Speaking post-match, Bellingham was clear where he ranked that finish, declaring: 'I think this was the best goal of my life.'.

He later elaborated to TNT Sports about his goal: 'They're [his goals] normally a lot closer, aren't they,' he joked.

SENSATIONAL JUDE BELLINGHAM 🤯Bellingham gives the hosts the lead with a magnificent volley 🔥 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB pic.twitter.com/WdP6ULx8wE.

Jude Bellingham (right) scored a stunning volley to inspire Real Madrid to beat PSV Eindhoven.

Bellingham came off the bench to put Real ahead with this beautiful right-footed volley.

PSV goalkeeper Matej Kovar could only watch on as the ball flew past him and go into the net.

'That one was a nice one, it popped up for me nicely and I just thought I'd hit it with the outside of my boot.

'I'm not one for smashing the ball too hard and it was a nice moment and key for the win as well.'.

Bellingham's performance, he also set up Vinicius Jr for the fifth goal, was acknowledged by Mourinho and Real captain Fede Valverde, who scored their equaliser, post-match too.

'Obviously Jude is a different type of player and he gave us what we didn't have in the first half,' Mourinho said. 'He changed the game, scored an incredible goal.'.

It has been revealed that valverde concurred declaring: 'He did well. We were struggling to keep the ball behind their midfielders and when Jude came in he gave us that tranquillity to control possession.'.

The strike comes a day after Daily Mail Sport reported that the 23-year-old is in advance talks over a new Real Madrid contract that will make him one of the best-paid players in Europe.

Madrid have been eager to tie down the in-form England midfielder beyond his current contract, understood to be worth around £12.5million a year after tax, which runs until 2029, in recognition of his performances.

Talks were initiated in September over an extension until 2031 and have been progressing well since with sources at Madrid confident they are close to reaching a conclusion.

Bellingham is in advance contract talks with Real Madrid over signing an extension until 2031.

Bellingham is expected to be handed improved terms to put him on par with team-mate Vinicius Jr, who agreed a newly introduced deal last summer reputedly on around £500,000 a week after tax.

As for Tuesday's win over PSV, Real are now top of the Champions League league phase standings after maintaining their 100 per cent record in the competition this season with a fifth-straight win.

According to recent reports, 1. Erling Haaland, Manchester City: £510,000 per week.

2. Kylian Mbappe, Real Madrid: £503,000 per week.

3. Vinicius Jr, Real Madrid: £500,000 per week.

Industry observers note that 4. Harry Kane, Bayern Munich: £402,000 per week.

In a recent development, 5. Virgil van Dijk, Liverpool: £350,000 per week.

However, they didn't have it all their own way as PSV took a deserved lead in the 32nd minute from the penalty spot, with 37-year-old captain Ivan Perisic showing all his experience, ignoring the whistles ringing out around the Bernabeu before sending Thibaut Courtois the wrong way.

They almost doubled their lead before the break as the unmarked Kodai Sano glanced a header off target as the visitors continued to cause Real serious problems.

Real equalised five minutes after the break, thanks to Arda Guler's quick-thinking, with the Turkish midfielder flicking a backheeled pass to Valverde in the area, who steered his first-time shot into the bottom corner.

Real's fans were on their feet 10 minutes later, scarcely believing what they had seen, while Bellingham's team-mates looked similarly shell-shocked.

Marc Cucurella walked away with his head in his hands in wonder while the other Real players rushed to congratulate the scorer.

Real took command after Bellingham's goal and punished a loose pass in the PSV defence, Guler finding the unmarked Mbappe to extend the France forward's scoring run to seven successive Champions League appearances.

Mbappe added his second before Vinicius rounded off a resounding victory from Bellingham's pass, underlining the Spanish side's credentials as serious contenders to take Paris Saint-Germain's crown.

Latest Update: AI in classrooms: Fighting the great 'dumbing down'

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1439 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium.
  • "I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW.
  • Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that jakob is 15 years old and attends a secondary school for more academic students, known in Germany as a gymnasium. He and his classmates have already been using artificial intelligence-enabled tools, or AI, for the last two and a half years.

"I had a French test today, and yesterday I had ChatGPT explain a lot of the topics to me again," the student told DW. Jakob isn't his real name, because he doesn't want to publicly admit he and many others of his age use AI to do their homework.

Math, German, English, chemistry and even physics: In one click, the solution or the path to a solution is available thanks to AI.

In science, this is called "cognitive outsourcing." Basically, the required thinking is shifted to another device, whether that's a calculator, notepad or a large language model (LLM) like ChatGPT.

Sources indicate that there's a difference with AI, though. A notepad or calculator can take over a step or two but rarely the whole thought process. That's not the same for an LLM, which can handle the entire problem-solving process.

Recent findings suggest that jakob admitted he's also had an AI help him with his homework. "But only when I was really stuck," he insisted. And he's also aware that it can become a problem when AI does all your homework. "The students who get good grades tend not to do that," he explained.

In a recent development, franziska Müller has been a German teacher for several decades and is presently teaching senior classes at a gymnasium. Her name has also been changed for privacy reasons.

"They can't even think for themselves anymore," she told DW, complaining about some of her classes.

Even in ordinary classes, some of the students type their questions into their tablets or phones, asking for AI assistance. And should they be called upon in class, she knows that they're reading out the answers that the AI has prepared for them and hoping nobody notices.

Sources indicate that müller believes students these days are less able to comprehend text. "Because they read less and let AI summarize almost everything for them," she noted.

Several studies have reached very similar conclusions.

In a recent development, that includes the latest PISA (Program for International Student Assessment) study from September. PISA, which is run by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, regularly evaluates the abilities of 15-year-old students around the world.

According to recent reports, "Students who report using AI chatbots get lower scores in science, on average, than those who don't use AI," Andreas Schleicher, the OECD director for education and skills, wrote in his report in October. "This includes using AI to summarize texts they had to read, conduct preliminary research on a fresh topic, or draft texts for writing assignments.".

Industry observers note that with participants from more than 90 countries, PISA is considered the largest international comparative study of 15-year-olds worldwide. This year, German 15-year-olds posted their lowest PISA scores in the 25-year history of the study.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

"The connections are complex and depend heavily on how generative AI is used, but the central insight is simple: Just as we don't get fit by watching sports but by doing sports ourselves, learning doesn't come from consuming content, but from the mind's productive cognitive engagement with latest material," Schleicher explained.

Put simply, those who don't exercise their brains risk becoming less intelligent.

US think tank, the Brookings Institution, has already argued that the risks of using AI in education outweigh the benefits.

Its own research, which included young participants from around the world, speaks of students losing "fundamental cognitive and durable skills as they increasingly rely on AI to perform learning's intellectual work," as well as the decline of critical thinking, memory, perseverance and independent judgment.

But what can be done against the power of ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and Meta AI?

Latest York Mayor Zohran Mamdani has banned the use of AI in public schools up to the eighth grade for the 2026 and 2027 school years — so that's up to about the age of 14 or 15.

Not everyone agrees this is the right thing to do. Julian Hinn, who teaches German to students aged between 15 and 18 in Germany, said class members can still use AI apps on their mobile phones. "And anyone who thinks they won't use it at home is ignoring reality," Hinn told DW.

Germany's annual JIM study, which tracks teenagers' media use and device ownership, supports that view.

In a recent development, 91% of young people surveyed in Germany, between the ages of 12 and 19, stated that they use at least one AI application. The study also reports that 74% use AI for homework and learning.

Recent findings suggest that the last JIM study actually dates back to 2024 so those percentages might be even higher now. Data on AI use in Asia, Latin America and the US from the Brookings study show similarly high figures.

According to recent reports, german politicians have recognized the problem. Although education in Germany is the responsibility of the individual federal states, the so-called Standing Conference of the Ministers of Education and Cultural Affairs, or KMK, has been issuing statements on the use of AI since 2024.

The KMK's statements have been rather vague though, saying only that students should be enabled to engage with AI in a critical, reflective and responsible manner.

Teachers and students alike are aware that AI can be a powerful support in the classroom.

"The AIs simply explain things much better than textbooks," said Jakob, adding that he'll often get an AI to explain basic concepts to him.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes teachers can't respond like an AI, Hinn conceded. "The AI ​​can respond much better to the language and needs of the students.".

That's why he thinks it's crucial to include AI in classes, starting from the 10th grade when students are around 15 or 16. Hinn doesn't think it should be introduced before that, when children's basic skills are still being developed.

According to recent reports, in more senior classes, Hinn will encourage his students to question the AI critically. "We look at the quality of the solutions," he explained.

In a recent development, german teacher Müller has also integrated some use of AI into her lessons for older students. But in some aspects of the class, she also bans it altogether so that her students can focus on thinking for themselves.

"I understand very well that it's tempting to use AI," she remarked.

Sources indicate that there are also other problems with AI in education. According to the Brookings study, students with basic skills can use AI to deepen their learning and progress faster.

Industry observers note that but for children with gaps in their knowledge, they tend to adopt AI's errors, outsource their thinking and then fall even further behind. In this way, AI can exacerbate preexisting inequalities.

The PISA study notes that children from more affluent backgrounds often have a better start, and AI can widen that gap.

This is called the Matthew effect — the name comes from the biblical verse Matthew 25:29, "for unto everyone that hath shall be given." It basically means that early success in learning leads to better progress in the future, while early struggles equal a growing lag over time.

In the age of AI, teachers have become more motivated to challenge students to think independently and to consider their own personal autonomy.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

Hinn, who also supervises the school newspaper, mentioned: "I always tell everyone, you can use AI but the feeling of having written an article with your own pen is spectacular.".

It has been revealed that both teachers also stress the idea of personal autonomy and responsibility. They believe this affects the students, especially because when they sit exams, they aren't allowed to use any aids or AI. And if they aren't able to solve their own problems, they will fail.

It's during exam time that the students really find out if they can solve those math, English or science problems by themselves.

Sources indicate that müller said one of her students recently confessed they were upset after a poor exam result. "He felt he simply couldn't think for himself anymore because of AI," she said.

This article was originally written in German.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

First launched in 1995, Mitreâs Ultimax ball promptly became a defining symbol in English football. A fixture on Premier League pitches throughout the 1990s, it made history as the first football to break the 100mph speed barrier.

Now, 30 years later, Mitre has reimagined the legendary ball, bringing it back with a modern twist.

The latest Ultimax Pro 30th Anniversary Ball merges the classic design with cutting-edge technology, celebrating its iconic status while setting a new standard for the next generation.

Recent findings suggest that while the ball retains the familiar 6-panel construction, the classic white, blue, and red colourway, and the unmistakable crown logo, itâs been upgraded with advanced features. Hyperflow grooves reduce drag and a sleek pearl finish offers a nod to traditional 30th-anniversary gifts. The interior also sees improvements, with Hyperfoam cushioning now enhanced for cleaner strikes and even more power.

To mark the milestone, Mitre has debuted the "The Next In Line" campaign, spotlighting the latest wave of football talent carrying on their family legacies.

The campaign features rising stars such as Raphaella Wright-Phillips, granddaughter of Arsenal icon Ian Wright, Ruben Butt, son of Manchester United legend Nicky Butt, and Jacob Fowler, whose father is Liverpoolâs own Robbie Fowler.

The trio, each in vintage 95/96 kits, embody the connection between the past and the future â just as the latest Ultimax Pro does itself.

Manchester United have reportedly been dealt a setback in their pursuit of Victor Osimhen, with the Nigerian striker increasingly unlikely to leave Galatasaray during the January transfer window despite renewed interest from Old Trafford.

The 27-year-old has established himself as one of Europe’s most prolific forwards since moving to Turkey, attracting attention from several leading clubs with his impressive goalscoring record.

According to a TEAMtalk report, Manchester United remain admirers of the Galatasaray forward as they explore opportunities to strengthen their attacking options.

The Red Devils have identified a new centre-forward as a priority ahead of the winter transfer window, particularly as Benjamin Sesko is currently struggling with an injury.

Osimhen has previously expressed a strong desire to experience Premier League football, making him an attractive option for United manager Mauricio Pochettino.

However, a January transfer appears increasingly complicated, with Galatasaray unwilling to lose their leading goalscorer midway through the campaign.

The Turkish champions have the Nigerian under contract until 2029 and are determined to retain his services as they pursue domestic and European success.

Sources indicate that Osimhen is comfortable remaining in Istanbul until the end of the season and would prefer to consider his options during the summer transfer window.

His importance to Galatasaray is reflected in his remarkable record of 69 goals and 19 assists in 85 appearances since arriving at the club.

Meanwhile, United are expected to explore alternative opportunities rather than spend considerable resources pursuing an unlikely January deal.

Monaco’s Folarin Balogun and Al-Ahli striker Ivan Toney are among the forwards who could attract attention from the Premier League giants.

A upcoming attacking addition could also influence Joshua Zirkzee’s future, with the Dutchman potentially allowed to leave if suitable reinforcements arrive.

Osimhen remains an attractive long-term option, but United may have to wait until next summer to pursue his signature.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Although coronary artery disease (CAD) genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci, most variants lie in non-coding regions, obscuring the causal gene programmes and cell types driving disease1,2.
  • According to recent reports, common diseases are driven by a multitude of factors and remain difficult to treat given the lack of a unified disease mechanism4.
  • Although population-scale GWAS offer great opportunity for target discovery, most identified variants lie within non-coding regions of the genome, making it difficult to dissect the causal cell types and molecular pathways13.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Although coronary artery disease (CAD) genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified hundreds of loci, most variants lie in non-coding regions, obscuring the causal gene programmes and cell types driving disease1,2. Here we performed single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of gene expression and chromatin accessibility in human coronary arteries from 44 people to construct a genome-wide single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map. We identified 11,269 chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTLs) across principal vascular cell types, including CAD-associated caQTLs in smooth muscle cells (SMCs). Using dynamic single-cell caQTL modelling3, we show that variant effects on chromatin vary across SMC states. For example, rs658956-mediated suppression of the FGGY-DT enhancer through disruption of an AP-1 motif is amplified as SMCs transition towards a fibromyocyte fate. We next performed genome-wide high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) in 15 human coronary arteries, showing that rs4887091 in the ADAMTS7 CAD locus has allele-dependent effects on CCCTC-binding factor occupancy and loop strength. Integrating Hi-C, Hi-C with chromatin immunoprecipitation and in vitro clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats interference (CRISPRi) nominated AMOTL2 as a distal SMC-specific CAD gene whose loss promotes proliferation and suppresses contractile identity. Finally, arrayed Perturb–seq of GWAS-nominated enhancers converged on extracellular matrix remodelling as a core SMC disease programme. Together, these findings provide a framework for mapping non-coding GWAS variants to cell types, chromatin states and gene programmes in human disease.

According to recent reports, common diseases are driven by a multitude of factors and remain difficult to treat given the lack of a unified disease mechanism4. Coronary artery disease (CAD) is among the most prevalent common chronic diseases, and numerous genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have now identified hundreds of variants linked to CAD risk. Although these results may potentially pave the way for upcoming therapeutic target discovery1,2,5,6, much of the translation from GWAS to therapeutic targets for CAD has been restricted to lipid-lowering drugs7,8. Large-scale clinical studies have demonstrated a persistent residual risk of CAD independent of lipid levels9,10, but we lack drugs that directly target disease pathways in the vessel wall due to an incomplete understanding of causal disease mechanisms. Leveraging human genetics to uncover new lipid-independent biological mechanisms and drug targets in CAD represents a tremendous unmet need and would be a principal milestone in translating population-scale GWAS findings to therapies for patients11,12.

Although population-scale GWAS offer great opportunity for target discovery, most identified variants lie within non-coding regions of the genome, making it difficult to dissect the causal cell types and molecular pathways13. The advent of single-cell sequencing technologies now allows for the profiling of human tissues in health and disease at unprecedented granularity14. Previous studies have used traditional single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) for detailed characterization of cell states in human tissue that drive disease15,16,17,18; however, these studies do not profile the non-coding genome, making it challenging to link GWAS variants to observed molecular changes. More recently, single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (ATAC) with sequencing (snATAC–seq) in human coronary arteries was conducted to link CAD GWAS variants to regulatory elements19. Although this represented an crucial advance in the field, the lack of complementary transcriptomic profiling rendered it challenging to nominate causal genes in vascular cell types. Furthermore, isolated snATAC–seq precludes the discovery of distal gene regulation as a driver of disease20, and there are presently no studies that profile the three-dimensional (3D) chromatin architecture in human coronary arteries to enable the investigation of these distal regulatory connections.

Herein we performed simultaneous multi-omic profiling of the transcriptome and epigenome in nuclei from 44 human coronary arteries to build a multi-omic enhancer–gene map of CAD. Collectively, these analyses identified CAD-associated regulatory variants and enhancer–gene links in smooth muscle cells (SMCs), motivating focused analysis of SMC state-dependent gene regulation. To expand insight into gene regulation across functionally heterogeneous SMC cell states, we used dynamic chromatin accessibility quantitative trait loci (caQTL) modelling to uncover cell-state-dependent pathogenicity of disease variants. To dissect the role of disease-associated variants in regulating larger scale gene networks, we performed genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries to link variants to distal genes and validated our findings using cell-specific high-throughput chromosome conformation capture (Hi-C) with chromatin immunoprecipitation (Hi-ChIP–seq) and in vitro CRISPRi. Finally, we performed Perturb–seq in human coronary artery SMCs (HCASMCs) to characterize functional mechanisms of repressing disease-associated enhancers and genes. Collectively, we provide a multi-omic map of human CAD by integrating transcriptomic, epigenetic and chromatin architecture to link disease-associated genetic variants with candidate disease-relevant cell types and target genes.

Recent findings suggest that we performed single-nucleus Multi-ome (RNA+ATAC) sequencing in 44 human coronary arteries from non-failing donors and patients with chronic heart failure isolated at the time of heart transplantation (Fig. 1a, Supplementary Fig. 1a and Supplementary Table 1). After quality control, we recovered 126,804 nuclei from 11 distinct cell types (Fig. 1b,c and Supplementary Fig. 1b–d). Using differential expression of canonical genes, we identified clusters corresponding to all main vascular cell types, including coronary artery SMCs (MYH11, ACTA2, ITGA8), endothelial cells (VWF, LDB2, PECAM1), fibroblasts (LAMA2, DCN, FBLN1) and myeloid cells (F13A1, CD163, MRC1) (Fig. 1b, Extended Data Fig. 1a–c and Supplementary Table 2). We used MACS2 to identify areas of open chromatin (‘peaks’) from the ATAC–seq data (Fig. 1e) and identified 143,743 cell-type-specific differentially accessible peaks (Extended Data Fig. 1d,e). Generally, cell-type clustering was concordant between the RNA and ATAC data. However, gene-expression data enabled the annotation of rarer cell types that were not captured by ATAC-based clustering alone (Supplementary Fig. 1e–g). Using differentially accessible peaks across cells, we also discovered cell-type-specific enrichment of transcriptional motifs such as SpiB and PU.1 in myeloid cells, MEF2B/C/D in SMCs and CCAAT/enhancer-binding protein in adipocytes (Supplementary Fig. 1h). We linked peaks to genes using a new supervised single-cell model called single-cell enhancer-to-gene (E2G) (scE2G)21 (Fig. 1d, Extended Data Fig. 2a–g and Supplementary Tables 3–14; Methods). We found that the non-immune cells had the greatest number of shared enhancers relative to myeloid cells (Fig. 1d) and that all cell types had a similar number of E2G links (Fig. 1e and Supplementary Table 3).

Notably, we found that cardiometabolic disease variants for CAD, systolic blood pressure (SBP) and diastolic blood pressure (DBP) were enriched in differentially accessible marker peaks specific to SMCs and endothelial cells (Fig. 1f). As a predominantly non-vascular trait, diabetes did not demonstrate enrichment of disease-associated variants (Fig. 1f).

It has been revealed that to boost our power for single-cell caQTL (sc-caQTL) discovery, we integrated our Multi-ome ATAC–seq data with available snATAC–seq data from human coronary arteries19 to create a meta-map of 88 samples and 245,562 nuclei across four ancestry groups (Extended Data Fig. 3a–f). We then used RASQUAL to identify pseudobulk caQTLs in four principal vascular cell types (SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells, fibroblasts) (Fig. 2a). At the 10% false discovery rate (FDR) threshold, we found 11,269 significant caQTL associations in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3g–i, Supplementary Fig. 2a–d and Supplementary Tables 15–26). Power, sensitivity, subsampling and runtime analyses are shown in Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3 and described in Supplementary Methods.

We further characterized caQTL variants to assess their regulatory potential. Lead caQTL variants were enriched strongly near the peaks they were predicted to regulate, consistent with a cis-regulatory mechanism (Extended Data Fig. 3j). We next overlapped our pseudobulk caQTLs and GTEx bulk arterial tissue eQTLs by cell type and found several hundred shared QTL variants in SMCs, endothelial cells, myeloid cells and fibroblasts (Extended Data Fig. 3i). Furthermore, we found a strong correlation in effect size between our SMC caQTLs and bulk coronary artery eQTLs from GTEx (Extended Data Fig. 3k). Finally, in SMCs we trained a convolutional neural net model (seq2PRINT22) that incorporates chromatin accessibility and ATAC footprinting to predict transcription factor binding probability at a base-pair resolution. We found that caQTL variants within accessible peaks had significantly higher predicted transcription factor binding probabilities compared with all other non-caQTL SNP sites within accessible peaks (P = 8.2 × 10−40, Wilcoxon rank sum) (Extended Data Fig. 3l).

To identify disease-associated caQTLs, we overlapped sc-caQTLs for each cell type with CAD GWAS variants (defined as lead variants associated with CAD at 1% FDR1 and variants in linkage disequilibrium with these at R2 ≥ 0.8 in the European population from 1000 Genomes Project; Supplementary Table 27), which yielded numerous disease-relevant cell-type-specific caQTLs (Extended Data Fig. 3m). For example, we found that rs7182567 was an SMC-specific caQTL that was also a GWAS variant (P = 5.4 × 10−26) and a bulk GTEx eQTL for ADAMTS7 in tibial artery (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Similarly, we found that rs8017642 is an endothelial cell-specific caQTL in the NEK9 locus (Extended Data Fig. 4b), whereas rs2337154 and rs1443120 are fibroblast- and myeloid-specific caQTLs, respectively (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d).

Industry observers note that next, we leveraged the paired RNA data to sub-cluster SMCs into transcriptionally distinct cell states, forming a continuum from ‘healthy’ contractile SMC states (SMC1–3) to de-differentiated ‘disease-associated’ SMC states including fibromyocytes (FMCs) and chondromyocytes (CMCs) (Extended Data Fig. 4e). Notably, we found that ADAMTS7 was expressed most highly in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 4e), indicating a role in disease regulation. To identify functionally distinct endothelial cell states, we mapped our data to a high-resolution scRNA-seq atherosclerosis atlas23 and identified four transcriptionally distinct endothelial subsets (Extended Data Fig. 4f). Notably, NEK9 was expressed in endothelial cells enriched with endothelium-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT) genes such as COL1A1 and FN1 (refs. 24,25) (Extended Data Fig. 4f,g). Pathway enrichment in the EMT population indicated increased EMT and stress-response signals (Extended Data Fig. 4h). Next, we created a gene set score comprised of 41 endothelial cell-specific genes thought to be associated causally with CAD26 that showed maximal enrichment in intimal endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4i). Similarly, we created a gene signature of a gene programme26 identified previously as driving CAD pathogenesis in endothelial cells (Programme 8) and found an enrichment of this programme in angiogenic and/or vasa vasorum endothelial cells (Extended Data Fig. 4j).

In a recent development, the CAD disease-associated variant rs658956 illustrates how a cell-type-specific caQTL can impart functional transcriptional changes. The variant is an SMC-specific and fibroblast-specific caQTL and regulates a putative enhancer element (chr. 1: 59169569–59170069), which is linked to the gene FGGY-DT in an SMC-specific manner by scE2G (Fig. 2c,d). Consistently, we found that rs658956 is also a coronary artery eQTL for FGGY-DT expression (P = 3.4 × 10−12) wherein the alternative allele (T) is associated with decreased expression relative to the reference allele (G) (Fig. 2e) and is also predicted to overlie a high probability transcription factor binding site (Fig. 2f). Motif-based transcription factor binding site analysis found that rs658956 is predicted to disrupt a core AP-1 (JUN/FOS) transcription factor binding motif (5′-TGAGTCA-3′) (Fig. 2g). Electrophoretic mobility shift assay (EMSA) demonstrated a binding shift in the reference allele sequence (containing G) that was not present in the alternative allele sequence (containing T) when these alleles were exposed to nuclear lysate from SMCs (Fig. 2h). Antibody supershift EMSA confirmed that the shifted AP-1 complex band consists of JUN and FOS transcription factors (Extended Data Fig. 4k). Together, these results suggest that the disease-associated variant rs658956 impacts transcription factor binding, thereby decreasing the chromatin accessibility of the enhancer and subsequently reducing FGGY-DT expression in a SMC-specific manner.

In a recent development, in atherosclerosis, SMCs undergo a well-characterized phenotypic switch from a contractile state to a fibroblast-like FMC phenotype16, driven by disease-associated transcriptional programmes. To characterize this transition, individual nuclei were assigned an FMC score based on FMC state marker genes for downstream modelling (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 5a–d). Notably, this FMC gene score is dynamic with disease across species, disease burden, pseudotime trajectory, in vitro HCASMC stress and transcriptional regulation (Extended Data Fig. 5e–k). To identify state-dependent caQTL effects, we used a Poisson mixed-effects (PME) single-cell model (Extended Data Fig. 6a–c; Methods). Applying this PME model to the lead variants of SMC-specific pseudobulk caQTLs, we identified 712 caQTLs whose effects were dynamic with respect to the FMC score (FDR ≤ 5%) (Supplementary Tables 29 and 30). Notably, eight of these dynamic caQTLs were also disease-associated variants. For example, rs658956 exhibited a significant interaction with FMC score (FDR-adjusted likelihood ratio test (LRT) P value = 2.36 × 10−4) (Fig. 2j,k). A negative interaction term indicates that, as the FMC score increased, the negative association between rs658956 and local chromatin accessibility was amplified (Fig. 2j,k). Using the scE2G map to link dynamic caQTL-related enhancer elements (caPeaks) to target genes, we found that extracellular matrix (ECM) remodelling was the most enriched pathway among linked genes (Extended Data Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Table 31). Notably, several of these genes linked to dynamic caPeaks were enriched in FMCs (Extended Data Fig. 6f and Supplementary Table 32). Similar state-dependent effects were observed at other CAD loci such as dynamic caQTL variant rs11838776 in the COL4A1 locus, suggesting that COL4A1 may play a role during transition toward an FMC state (Extended Data Fig. 6g–k). Collectively, these dynamic analyses demonstrate that disease-associated variants can exert cell-state-dependent regulatory effects on chromatin accessibility.

To map CAD disease-associated variants to cell types and genes in an unbiased fashion, we built a disease-relevant single-cell variant-to-enhancer-to-gene map (scV2E2G) integrating cell-type-specific regulatory elements, CAD GWAS variants, scE2G links and caQTLs21,27 (Fig. 3a; Methods).

Overlapping scE2G with sc-caQTLs provides a high-fidelity set of predicted variants that may be driving disease by directly regulating intermediate molecular traits in a cell-type-specific manner.

It has been revealed that focusing on the 325 genes linked to SMC enhancers harbouring CAD GWAS variants, we performed several enrichment analyses. These analyses found that these linked genes were over-represented in nearest lead genes from CAD and myocardial infarction GWAS, identified GATA2 as the most enriched transcription factor and highlighted collagen and ECM remodelling as key biological processes (Extended Data Fig. 7a and Supplementary Tables 37–39). Correlation analysis between gene expression and FMC score identified FN1, COL4A1, COL4A2, MFGE8 and MYO9B—all known CAD-associated genes implicated in ECM remodelling—among the most highly correlated transcripts (Extended Data Fig. 7b and Supplementary Table 40). Notably, the enhancer harbouring variant rs7246865 emerged as potentially vital in disease, acting as both a cell-state dynamic caPeak and pseudobulk caPeak in SMCs with a high-confidence scE2G link (Fig. 3b). We confirmed this predicted link experimentally using CRISPRi in HCASMCs. Repressing the rs7246865-containing enhancer significantly reduced MYO9B expression relative to a non-targeting control (Fig. 3c), consistent with previous functional validation at this locus1. Furthermore, CRISPRi validated scE2G predictions in SMCs for three additional loci near genes LOXL1, NAV1 and PALLD; enhancer repression altered gene expression significantly at each of these loci relative to non-targeting controls (Extended Data Fig. 7c–e).

According to recent reports, to further validate scE2G links, we performed arrayed CRISPRi Perturb–seq in HCASMCs, delivering individual sgRNAs to target either the transcription start site (TSS) or the nominated enhancer at eight CAD GWAS loci (Fig. 3d, Supplementary Fig. 4 and Supplementary Table 41). Alongside transcriptional profiling, we measured SMC proliferation by live-cell imaging, revealing that several perturbations (including ADAMTS7, CFDP1 and COL4A1) and significantly reduced proliferation rate, with enhancer knockdowns generally phenocopying their cognate TSS perturbations (Fig. 3e, Extended Data Fig. 8a and Supplementary Table 42). Following quality control, we retained 76,179 cells and confirmed robust, perturbation-specific transcriptional responses, with selective target-gene knockdown, stronger effects for TSS than enhancer perturbations and separation from non-targeting controls (Extended Data Fig. 8b–j).

Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) revealed locus-specific pathway enrichments: BMP1 and ADAMTS7 knockdowns strongly enriched MYC and E2F target-gene sets, whereas CFDP1 and COL4A1 knockdowns suppressed interferon response pathways, indicating distinct downstream transcriptional consequences across CAD loci (Extended Data Fig. 9a). Consensus non-negative matrix factorization identified six biologically interpretable programmes: inflammation, ECM remodelling, vascular remodelling, interferon response and two proliferative programmes corresponding to S and M phase (Extended Data Fig. 9b,c and Supplementary Tables 43 and 44). Notably, the ECM remodelling programme showed the strongest positive correlation with the FMC module score, with enhancer knockdowns of CFDP1, MYO9B and BMP1 exhibiting the highest mean FMC scores (Extended Data Fig. 9d–h). Programme-level analysis further revealed that COL4A1 and its enhancer were the strongest drivers of the inflammation programme, whereas the MRAS and CFDP1 enhancer perturbations modulated both inflammation and ECM remodelling (Fig. 3f).

Finally, robust rank aggregation (RRA) across pseudobulk DESeq2 profiles revealed a convergent gene programme dominated by downregulation of several collagen genes (COL3A1, COL4A1, COL5A1, COL6A1–A3) and TIMP2, alongside the upregulation of metabolic and stress-response genes (Fig. 3g, Extended Data Fig. 9i and Supplementary Table 45). Pathway enrichment of this convergent programme identified EMT, tumour necrosis factor signalling through nuclear factor κB, and mammalian target of rapamycin complex 1 signalling as the top enriched terms (Fig. 3h). Collectively, these findings implicate a shared regulatory framework that governs SMC phenotypic states across independent, disease-associated loci.

According to recent reports, to investigate how disease-associated variants may influence broader gene networks through chromatin looping, we performed genome-wide Hi-C in 15 human coronary arteries to construct large-scale chromatin networks (Fig. 4a, Extended Data Fig. 10a–f and Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6). To further complement Hi-C in bulk tissue, we performed H3K27Ac Hi-ChIP–seq in cultured human coronary artery smooth muscle cells and endothelial cells. Comparing the number of enhancer–gene connection overlap by method, we found that scE2GMulti-ome and Hi-ChIP yielded the highest number of enhancer–gene connections, with a smaller fraction from bulk coronary tissue Hi-C (Supplementary Fig. 7). We then identified groups of genomic loci that interact preferentially with one another in specific chromatin networks termed ‘mosaics’ (Fig. 4a; Methods). We identified 5,130 mosaics containing 11,494 protein-coding genes. Notably, mosaics harbouring a disease-associated variant exhibited significantly higher structural complexity, containing an average of 25 loops compared with 14 loops in non-disease-associated mosaics (P = 1.7 × 10−17) (Fig. 4b). This approach provides a framework for mapping disease-associated variants to a catalogue of genes regulated distally through interconnected chromatin networks (Supplementary Tables 46–49).

It has been revealed that next, we performed CTCF ChIP–seq in HCASMC to prioritize disease-associated SMC enhancers that are bound by CTCF. Of all CAD disease-associated variants, 498 overlapped CTCF peaks, including 200 within accessible chromatin regions. CAD-associated variants were enriched significantly at CTCF-bound regions above permutation-based expectation (1.25-fold, P = 0.02; Extended Data Fig. 10g).

Industry observers note that among the top-ranking regulatory mosaics, we identified mosaic-1664, which contains the CAD-associated variant rs4887091 located within an SMC enhancer (Fig. 4c). In this mosaic, we found an 800-kb boundary loop exhibiting a strong rs4887091 genotype-dependent increase in contact strength for the alternate allele (C) relative to the reference allele (T) (Fig. 4d). Specifically, the loop strength increased in a dose-dependent manner when quantified across all samples, where there was minimal contact strength in homozygotes (T|T), moderate strength in heterozygotes (T|C, C|T) and highest strength in homozygotes (C|C) (Fig. 4e). Phased genotypes confirmed increased looping strength on the C allele (P = 3.1 × 10−3) (Fig. 4f).

Recent findings suggest that to characterize the regulatory architecture of rs4887091 within mosaic-1664, we identified all genes linked to the SMC enhancer containing rs4887091: Hi-C identified a boundary loop containing ADAMTS7, MORF4L1, CHRNA3, IDH3A, ACSBG1, CIB2, SH2D7 and TBC1D2 promoters (Fig. 4d), whereas scE2G identified ADAMTS7 (the nearest gene) (Fig. 4g). Consistent with ADAMTS7 being a functional target of this regulatory element, CRISPRi Perturb–seq targeting the rs4887091-containing enhancer reduced ADAMTS7 expression in HCASMCs (Extended Data Fig. 8f). CTCF ChIP–seq in HCASMCs demonstrated that rs4887091 overlaps a CTCF binding site (Fig. 4g). Furthermore, motif-based transcription factor binding site analysis found that rs4887091, which changes the reference (T) to alternate (C) allele, is predicted to create a core CTCF binding motif (Fig. 4h). Consistent with this prediction, haplotype-resolved CTCF ChIP–seq demonstrated allelic dosage-dependent increases in CTCF occupancy on the C allele (P = 0.0003) (Fig. 4i). Validation at control loci and orthogonal TaqMan genotyping confirmed the accuracy of the haplotype-resolved CTCF occupancy measurements (Extended Data Fig. 10h–j). Together, these data support a model in which rs4887091 creates an allele-specific CTCF binding site associated with increased local chromatin loop strength, although the effect of this loop alteration on gene expression remains to be established.

In a recent development, although our scE2G predictions are limited to enhancer–gene interactions within a cis-window, leveraging Hi-C data can link CAD GWAS variants to distal genes. For the loops present in all 15 samples, we catalogued genes linked to a CAD GWAS variant through direct chromatin contact between putative enhancers and promoters and identified 11 such genes: ANTXR1, ARMC12, CNNM2, FKBP5, CAPG, SH2D6, AMOTL2, NUAK2, RGS1, PLCL1 and FOXC2 (Fig. 5a). Among these, ANTXR1, CAPG, SH2D6, AMOTL2, NUAK2 and RGS1 are not the nearest genes. As an example, the CAD-associated variant rs9876658 was linked to AMOTL2 through a direct Hi-C contact. rs9876658 falls within a snATAC–seq peak in SMCs, endothelial cells and fibroblasts (but not myeloid cells) highlighting stroma-specific regulation (Fig. 5b). H3K27ac ChIP–seq showed that rs9876658 overlapped a H3K27ac peak in SMCs but not in endothelial cells (Fig. 5b). Hi-ChIP–seq further identified a direct loop between the rs9876658-containing enhancer and the AMOTL2 promoter in SMCs but not in endothelial cells (Fig. 5b). Collectively, these analyses predict that the enhancer containing rs9876658 functionally regulates expression of AMOTL2 in SMCs but not in endothelial cells.
